AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: This study describes the association between frequency of bicycling for active transportation and modifiable cardiometabolic risk factors in the Minneapolis-Saint Paul (MSP) metropolitan area.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: We conducted an online survey from a convenience sample of likely bicycle commuters.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Participants were e-mailed invitations including a link to the online survey.

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: Participants (n = 1450, 15.6% response rate) were residents of the 7-county MSP metropolitan area aged 20 to 64 years.

AbstractText.Label: MEASURES
AbstractText.content: Participants reported frequency of commute and destination cycling from April to September and October to March, prevalent cardiometabolic risk factors, and demographic covariates.

AbstractText.Label: ANALYSIS
AbstractText.content: We performed logistic regressions for associations between average weekly transportation bicycling and self-reported prevalent obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high triglycerides. We used Poisson regression for the count of cardiometabolic risk factors. All models were adjusted for age, sex, race, smoking, alcohol consumption, and other physical activity, with random intercepts by zip code.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Self-reported bicycling frequency is associated with significantly lower odds of prevalent obesity, hypertension, and high triglycerides. Three bicycling trips per week is associated with 20% fewer (95% confidence interval: 12%-28%) cardiometabolic risk factors.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Bicycling frequency is inversely associated with cardiometabolic risk factors. These results provide empirical support for the promotion of active transportation as public health policy.
